description: We’re a group of IT students from Universidad Politécnica de Querétaro (UPQ), and this is our first hackathon. We enjoy building things, and we learn fast by doing. We’re not space experts, and that’s okay: we’re curious, we work well together, and we want to build something we’re proud of. We’d especially value teammates who are strong in design, data analysis or storytelling.
summary: Flame in Freefall Explorer is an evidence-first dashboard and AI assistant for NASA's microgravity combustion data. It brings together 403 real tests from two NASA Physical Sciences Informatics investigations, FLEX (PSI-69) and BASS-II (PSI-25), and lets anyone check which atmospheres were actually tested, which were not, and how the flames behaved. Choose a space scenario (ISS cabin, Moon base, lunar habitat, exploration atmosphere, spacesuit) or set your own oxygen and pressure, and the site ranks the most relevant tests, shows how many are exact or near matches, and states what the data cannot tell us. For example, ISS cabin air has 49 exact matches, while the lunar-habitat, exploration and spacesuit atmospheres have none. A built-in assistant answers only from these records, cites its sources and says "No data" instead of guessing. The site does not simulate or predict fire: it makes the gaps in the evidence visible, so that decisions about spacecraft and habitat atmospheres can be better informed.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Flame in Freefall Explorer is a static website plus an optional AI assistant that makes NASA's microgravity combustion records easy to explore and, above all, honest about what they do not cover. It uses 403 tests: 274 from FLEX (PSI-69) and 129 from BASS-II (PSI-25).

- Dashboard: pick a scenario (Earth/ISS, Moon base, NASA lunar habitat, Exploration, Spacesuit) or "Custom" to set oxygen, pressure and fuel. The page shows how many tests match exactly (±1% O2, ±0.5 psi) or nearby, and what the nearest tests show.

- Experiments: search, filter and sort all 403 tests, ordered by relevance to the chosen atmosphere with a visible formula (exact first, then by distance in tolerance units, no hidden weights), plus a detail panel for each test with its DOI and limitations.

- Coverage and Gaps: which atmospheres were tested (20 of 30 FLEX grid cells; 26 of 129 BASS-II outcomes stated) and what is missing, for example no test below 10.2 psi or above 34% O2.

- Indicators: tests, investigations, complete vs. partial records (283 / 120), scenario coverage and conditions without evidence, each with its denominator.

- Assistant: answers only questions about this data and the site, cites its sources, shows its n and warnings, and answers "No data" when the records do not cover a question.

HOW IT WORKS

NASA PSI data are cleaned into SQLite tables and exported as static JSON that the React site reads, so the public link needs no server. An optional FastAPI backend adds a local assistant: the model only chooses a whitelisted query and phrases at most three sentences; the code adds citations and test IDs, and a verifier rejects any number that is not in the query result, any forecast language, URLs or off-topic content, falling back to a fixed template. The public site runs the "Basic" mode (rules and templates, no model). "Flash" (llama3.2:3b) and "Medium" (qwen3:8b) run locally with Ollama on the team's laptop for demos.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

For mission planners, fire-safety engineers, researchers and students, it turns two dense datasets into a clear picture of what evidence exists for a given spacecraft or habitat atmosphere, and where new tests are needed. Four of the five space scenarios we checked have no exact test, which is the key finding.

WHAT IT DOES NOT DO (by design)

It does not simulate, predict or rate safety. FLEX extinction percentages are descriptive, not probabilities. BASS-II "not stated" is not "not extinguished". Results with n<5 are flagged. All data are microgravity (ISS); there are no partial- or normal-gravity tests. Flame visuals are conceptual illustrations. Three scenario sources (lunar habitat, exploration, spacesuit) are labelled "Unverified source".

TOOLS

React, TypeScript and Vite (front end); Python, FastAPI, Pydantic and SQLite (back end and data); Ollama with llama3.2:3b and qwen3:8b (optional local AI); Vitest, pytest and Playwright (more than 870 Python tests, almost 500 front-end tests, and an audit script that recomputes every number shown against the database with 0 discrepancies); Lighthouse (mobile 95+ performance, 100 accessibility). Hosted as a static site on Netlify. Code: Apache-2.0. Data: NASA PSI, CC0-1.0.

CREATIVITY

Instead of another prediction tool, the project treats missing evidence as the result: scenarios with zero tests are shown as findings, the assistant refuses to guess, and every figure is traceable to a test and a DOI.

USE OF SI (AI)

- Anthropic Claude (an LLM assistant) helped write most of the code, tests and documentation under the team's direction, and helped design the interface.

- AI-written rules extracted the outcomes of 26 of 129 BASS-II tests from the source text; they are labelled "AI-extracted" on the site and in the data (ai_* fields).

- The optional local assistant uses Ollama models (llama3.2 and qwen3), always checked by the verifier.

- Not fully reviewed: parts of the back end and front end code, 3 low-confidence BASS-II outcomes and 3 unverified scenario sources. No images, video or audio in the project are AI-generated. No NASA logos or branding are used.

TEAM AND LINKS

Team St4rs R1pp3rs (Stars Rippers): Baz, Fer, Yael, Carlos and Jovanny, students of Information Technology Engineering at Universidad Politécnica de Querétaro. Source code: https://github.com/who-is-baz/stars-rippers-flame-in-freefall
